method: Targeted content sample, not a random or statistically representative audit. Compare the actual reference entries and, for Psittacara, the naming author’s explanation. Read German, English and Dutch editorial versions together; distinguish word origin, bird identification, historical spelling and naming intention.

cases.finding: Vigors explicitly names his bridging group after parakeet-macaws. Prioritise that documented intention over Jobling’s later Greek-head analysis; remove the blanket uncertainty flag.
The Greek mythological name is documented; uncertainty concerns its application to the bird, not the identity of the source name.
Distinguish Latin cista (basket) from Greek kistos/kisthos (rockrose); Latin -cola/colere is shared. Retain uncertainty about the intended first component.
The previous main citation to BOU did not support the diver analysis. Cite Jobling for diver and BOU for its alternative crest-bearer interpretation; retain uncertainty.
Replace an unsupported claim about the usual interpretation with explicit attribution to Jobling; distinguish -kephalos from kephale. Original naming intention was not independently established.
Grey-headed is the documented intended sense. Greek kirrhos is only a proposed derivation and denotes yellowish colour; do not assert that root as established.

Regulus refers to the Goldcrest’s epithet; little king is its literal meaning, not an independently supported alternative etymology for proregulus. Pallas’s original naming motive was not checked; retain uncertainty.
Separate the historical hiaticola form from later diminutive-like remodelling. Replace the unavailable WNVE main reference with consulted sources; retain uncertainty about the competing analyses.
Qualify the diminutive reading; add the competing historical hypothesis and uncertainty flag.
No explained derivation at introduction; proposed Greek roots and anagrams must remain conjectural.
Melas is black, but koruphos is an obscure ancient bird name, with possible confusion with lark/crested-bird words; black crown is too categorical.
Oura means tail; aiginthos is an ancient bird name of uncertain identification. Uncertainty does not invalidate the tail component.
Ancient erithakos/Latin erithacus is established; a deeper decomposition must not be presented as settled.
Hupolais names an unidentified ancient ground-nesting bird; further analyses are proposals.
Swainson’s string-of-twilight explanation is reported with attribution; later competing accounts justify retaining the uncertainty flag.
Blue is identifiable; the second component has competing accounts. The current cautious formulation is justified.
The Tupí proposals and lack of an explanation by Spix justify retaining cautious language.
Mouse-parrot and the spelling problem are documented; do not reinterpret myio- as fly.
Dendron (tree) and kopos (striking), with kopto as the verb, support the current explanation.
The current text marks the tail analysis as historical and the autonomous cilla meaning as spurious; it does not assert a resolved ultimate etymology.

limitations: This review covers 20 selected terms, not all 1,237 terms. Source agreement within this sample does not independently establish every historical naming intention.
Uncertainty flags distinguish several kinds of uncertainty; explanatory prose identifies what is unknown. Retained flags do not imply all components are unknown.
Wember (2005) remains further reading only: its full text was unavailable and no finding is attributed to it.
WNVE’s hiaticula page could not be retrieved during this review; it was not counted as a consulted source.
This is a content review. The separate earlier visual review records its own version and scope.
